Variadic ports should still feel like ports.

Five actual SystemSketch paint states for the same saved *args/**kwargs board. Each keeps the single DEF-owned label, physical cable endpoints, normal 18px port typography, and inward-facing socket arrows. Only the surrounding connective grammar and the rare inspector surface vary.

Fixed before comparison

These are gates, not options to trade away.

Invariant contract

  • One group spelling only: *overlays or **options.
  • Each source expression remains a normal, independently cableable input port.
  • The socket cue points inward; it never implies an outbound cable.
  • No board schema or authoring gesture changes in this review.

Evidence

  • Each card embeds actual headless-Chrome captures of the identical review board.
  • Browser proof checked two group labels, six socket teeth, unchanged controls, and no duplicated type token in every mode.
  • The live link opens the actual renderer on this isolated review track.

What to judge

35%Normal port cadence
25%Inward socket semantics
20%Dense-run legibility
15%Visual quietness
5%Rare inspector authoring

Unranked live atlas

The five are deliberately shown in prototype order. Click “Pick / splice” as you inspect; no app state is changed.

V1

Continuous inward rail

A one-pixel spine links the existing ports; a tiny arrowhead at each port points into the Block and the one label occupies the middle ordinary-port slot.

Favors Best when a compact call face must keep its ordinary-port cadence.

Costs The group boundary is intentionally subtle at a distance.

Open V1 live on the review board ↗
V2

Capped socket family

Terminal caps make the rail look like a single contained family, while every arrow still points inward and the label keeps a normal baseline.

Favors Best when rapid scanning of dense, adjacent groups beats visual quietness.

Costs The cap and inspector card bring the most extra chrome.

Open V2 live on the review board ↗
V3

Dotted continuity

A dashed spine supplies the lightest possible grouping punctuation; solid inward arrows preserve the direction at the sockets themselves.

Favors Best when an already-busy board needs the grouping to recede.

Costs At low zoom the dotted spine may under-signal the family.

Open V3 live on the review board ↗
V4

DEF-rooted rail

The group label takes the first ordinary-port box and the rail descends from it, prioritising source-order signature reading over vertical centring.

Favors Best when the UI should foreground definition order.

Costs The label is no longer optically centred across a multi-slot run.

Open V4 live on the review board ↗
V5

Yoke ladder

A stronger bracket-and-ladder frame makes the run unmistakable while keeping the centre label in the exact normal-port position.

Favors Best when runs appear beside many normal ports and must read in one glance.

Costs The canvas frame has more visual weight than the continuous rail.

Open V5 live on the review board ↗

AI splice: V1 canvas rail + V5 tucked inspector.

V1 most faithfully fulfils the “looks exactly like a port” request: the label uses the middle normal port box and the rail is only a connection. V5’s inspector is the best companion because this metadata is rare and still fully authorable. Keep V2’s terminal cap in reserve if dense boards prove the V1 rail too quiet.

Decision hinge. The one useful question is whether a dense call face needs an explicit bounded family at a glance. If yes, take V2’s cap; if not, V1 is the most disciplined expression of the chosen model.
